prompt: Why does the time of one exact search grow with the number of stored vectors?
hint: Look at the last column brute.py printed.

choices.text: Because sorting the scores is the expensive part
choices.why: brute.py does not even sort them all: argpartition picks the ten best. The work that grows is the dot products.

choices.text: Each query reads all of them, one multiply-add per coordinate
choices.why: Right. The multiply-adds column is the vector count times 384, and the time follows it.

choices.text: Because random vectors are slower to compare than embedded texts
choices.why: The arithmetic is the same whatever the numbers mean; that is why brute.py could use random ones.

choices.text: Because the query's vector gets longer as the collection grows
choices.why: The query has 384 numbers whatever the collection's size; it is the number of vectors it meets that grows.

prompt: In `brute.py`, ten times the vectors took 8.9 times as long from 10,000 to 100,000, but 22 times as long from 100,000 to 1,000,000. What is the likeliest reason?
hint: Look at the memory column.

choices.text: A million vectors need more multiply-adds per vector
choices.why: Every vector costs 384 multiply-adds at every size; the last column grows exactly tenfold.

choices.text: argpartition becomes the slow step past a hundred thousand scores
choices.why: Picking ten from a list is cheap next to computing the list; nothing in the output points at it.

choices.text: 1536 MB per query: memory sets the pace
choices.why: Right. Every query reads all 1536 MB; at that size the processor waits for memory, and the multiplications are no longer the limit.

choices.text: The program switched to several threads for the large size
choices.why: brute.py fixes one thread before importing NumPy, for every size.

prompt: A library's help centre has 5,000 articles embedded with MiniLM and answers about three searches a second. Which search should it use?
hint: Compare with the 10,000 row of brute.py.

choices.text: Exact search: at this size it is fast and never misses
choices.why: Right. brute.py searched twice as many vectors in 0.66 ms on one core; an index would add building and tuning for nothing.

choices.text: An approximate index, because exact search is only for testing
choices.why: Exact search is the method that returns the true nearest vectors; it is the right choice whenever reading everything is cheap enough.

choices.text: A hosted vector database, because 5,000 vectors do not fit in memory
choices.why: 5,000 vectors of 384 float32 numbers take under 8 MB.

choices.text: Keyword search, because embeddings are too slow at three searches a second
choices.why: The search over 5,000 vectors takes well under a millisecond; three a second is nothing.

prompt: How many multiply-adds does one exact search take over 50,000 vectors of 384 numbers?
hint: One per number stored.

prompt: How many megabytes do 2,000,000 vectors of 384 float32 numbers take, counting a megabyte as 1,000,000 bytes?
hint: brute.py printed 1536 MB for one million.

prompt: The help centre's vectors are in a NumPy matrix and their ids in a separate list. A row is inserted into the matrix and not into the list. What happens?
hint: Row numbers are the only link between the two.

choices.text: NumPy raises an error because the two lengths differ
choices.why: NumPy knows nothing about the list; nothing compares their lengths unless you write the check.

choices.text: From that row on, searches name the wrong articles
choices.why: Right. The match between rows and ids is by position, and it shifted silently. A store with ids keeps them in the record.

choices.text: Only the new row is wrong; the others still match their ids
choices.why: Every row after the inserted one moved by one, so every id after it points at a neighbour's vector.

choices.text: The scores change, but the ranking stays correct
choices.why: The scores are right for the vectors; it is the names attached to them that are wrong.

prompt: `vectors.npy` held 40 vectors of 384 `float32` numbers and was 61568 bytes. What are the 128 bytes beyond 40 × 1,536?
hint: Every .npy file starts the same way.

choices.text: The ids of the 40 articles
choices.why: The ids are in records.json; the .npy file holds only the array.

choices.text: An index that speeds up the search
choices.why: The small store has no index; its search reads every vector.

choices.text: The vector length of each record, stored for checking
choices.why: Forty lengths of 4 bytes would be 160 bytes, and the store keeps no lengths: it normalises instead.

choices.text: NumPy's header in front of the array
choices.why: Right. It records the shape and the number type, so np.load can rebuild the array.

prompt: How many bytes would `vectors.npy` be for 1,000 MiniLM vectors, with the same 128-byte header?
hint: Each vector is 384 numbers of 4 bytes.

prompt: Match each part of a record to what it is for.
hint: One description is a property of the collection, not of a record.

pairs.right: The join back to the source
The only part the search compares
What a person reads after the search

right_distractors: The model every vector in it came from

prompt: `refuse.py` searched with an all-MiniLM-L6-v2 vector but said `model="lab-minilm"`, labembed's name for the same model, and the store refused. Why is refusing the right behaviour?
hint: What could the store accept if it ignored names?

choices.text: Because lab-minilm gives different vectors from all-MiniLM-L6-v2
choices.why: labembed runs the same minilm.py; the vectors are the same. The refusal is about the name, not the numbers.

choices.text: Ignoring names would let another model's vectors through silently
choices.why: Right. The store compares names because it cannot compare weights, and a name that differs is the only warning it gets.

choices.text: Because the vector's dimension did not match the collection's
choices.why: Both are 384; the first refusal in refuse.py was the dimension one, with WordLlama's 256.

choices.text: Because searches must use the newest record's model
choices.why: The rule is per collection, not per record: every record in it came from all-MiniLM-L6-v2.

prompt: Marginalia's collection was created to compare by dot product of unit vectors. Somebody wants Euclidean distance instead. What has to happen?
hint: Which three things does a collection fix once?

choices.text: Pass a different metric with each query
choices.why: The comparison belongs to the collection: Chroma takes it as a space at creation and pgvector builds it into the index.

choices.text: Re-embed the articles with a model trained for distances
choices.why: The model is not the problem; the same vectors work with either comparison.

choices.text: Create a new collection
choices.why: Right. A new one, with the new comparison: it is fixed at creation, like the model and the dimension. For unit vectors the ranking would not even change, as lesson 2 showed.

choices.text: Edit the metric field of every record
choices.why: Records carry no metric; it is a property of the whole collection.

prompt: Besides the model and the comparison, a collection fixes at creation how many numbers every vector has: its ___.
hint: MiniLM's is 384.

prompt: After `delete("h18")`, `writes.py` printed `rows 41 alive 39`. What is in the row that held h18?
hint: The delete changed one flag.

choices.text: Its vector, marked dead, until the next save
choices.why: Right. A tombstone: still multiplied by every query and then discarded, until save() writes only the live rows.

choices.text: Nothing: the row was removed and the others moved up
choices.why: Then the rows would be 40. They stayed at 41, because moving rows is what the tombstone avoids.

choices.text: A vector of zeros, so it scores zero against every query
choices.why: The vector is untouched; it is the alive flag that keeps it out of the results, with a score of minus infinity.

choices.text: The edited h15, which took the free row
choices.why: The edit was appended as a new row before the delete; nothing reuses a dead row.

prompt: Why do vector databases mark a deleted record instead of removing it at once?
hint: Think about what removing it from the middle would disturb.

choices.text: So that a delete can be undone later
choices.why: Some may offer that, but it is not the reason; a delete is meant to stick, and compaction makes it permanent.

choices.text: Removing means moving rows or relinking an index; a mark is instant
choices.why: Right. The cost is deferred to a compaction or a rebuild, done once for many deletes.

choices.text: Because the law requires keeping deleted data for a time
choices.why: Nothing in how a store works depends on that; if anything, personal data has to be removed for real, which compaction does.

choices.text: Because a deleted vector still improves the scores of its neighbours
choices.why: A dead row is discarded from every result; it adds work and nothing else.

prompt: Why is the upsert the usual write in vector databases?
hint: Think of a job that re-embeds everything every night.

choices.text: It is faster than an insert because it skips the vector
choices.why: An upsert carries the vector like any write; the difference is what happens when the id exists.

choices.text: It recomputes the vector from the text by itself
choices.why: Neither tinystore nor most databases embed on upsert; the caller passes the vector, which is why it can be stale.

choices.text: A write is safe to repeat, existing id or not
choices.why: Right. The nightly job upserts all 40 articles without first asking which ones exist.

choices.text: It deletes the old vector from memory at once
choices.why: In tinystore the old row stays as a tombstone until save(); rows went from 40 to 41.

prompt: To save an API call, a developer rewrites h15 to say refunds are now given only as store credit, and upserts the new text with the vector already stored. What does the help centre do afterwards?
hint: Which of the two arguments does the search compare?

choices.text: The store notices the mismatch and refuses the upsert
choices.why: upsert checks the dimension and nothing else; no store can tell whether a vector belongs to a text.

choices.text: The search finds h15 for questions about store credit
choices.why: That would need the new text's vector. The stored vector still describes refunds to the card.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since a vector and its text are stored together
choices.why: Stored together is not computed together: the text changed and its vector did not.

choices.text: Card-refund questions still find h15, which now says store credit only
choices.why: Right. The vector answers for the old text and the person reads the new one. Re-embed in the same step as every text change.

prompt: A write that replaces the record when its id exists and adds it when it does not is called an ___.
hint: Update and insert, in one word.

prompt: Put in order what happened to the gift article, h18, across `index.py` and `writes.py`.
hint: It was on disk twice: once with it, once without.
items: Upserted with its vector and saved by index.py
Loaded back from disk by writes.py
Marked dead by delete, row still in the array
Left out of the files when save() compacted
trap: The delete did not remove the row: rows stayed at 41 until the save.

prompt: In `path.py`, which step of the query took the most time?
hint: Read the three timings.

choices.text: Searching the 39 vectors
choices.why: That took 0.155 ms, a rounding error beside the first step at this size.

choices.text: Embedding the question
choices.why: Right. 9.043 ms: running the model on the question costs more than everything after it.

choices.text: Fetching the texts by id
choices.why: 0.005 ms: a lookup in a list is the cheapest step.

choices.text: Applying the language filter
choices.why: The filter is part of the search call, which took 0.155 ms in total.

prompt: The same store grows to a million vectors and keeps exact search. Using this lesson's measurements, which step would now dominate a query?
hint: brute.py timed a million on one core.

choices.text: Embedding the question, which grows with the collection
choices.why: The question is one text whatever the collection's size; its cost stays near the 9.043 ms path.py measured.

choices.text: Fetching the texts, because there are a million of them
choices.why: Only the top few are fetched, by id, whatever the size.

choices.text: None: all three grow by the same factor
choices.why: Only the search reads every vector; the other two do not depend on the count.

choices.text: The search, at about 129 ms
choices.why: Right. brute.py measured 129.16 ms for a million; that is the step an approximate index replaces.

prompt: Put the steps of a query in a vector database in order.
hint: The text a person reads comes last, through the id.
items: Embed the question with the collection's model
Drop the candidates that fail the filter
Rerank the survivors, if a reranker is used
Fetch the texts of the ids that remain
trap: The texts are not fetched before the search: the search answers with ids, and only those ids are looked up.

prompt: Marginalia moves its help centre to 5,000 articles, embeds questions through a hosted API, and customers say search feels slow. Where should the investigation start?
hint: Which step grows with the collection, and which one crosses the internet?

choices.text: Add an approximate index, since the search is always the slow part
choices.why: At 5,000 vectors exact search takes well under a millisecond; path.py showed the search was the small step.

choices.text: Fetch fewer texts per query
choices.why: Fetching by id took 0.005 ms; it is the cheapest step.

choices.text: Time the embedding call, round trip included
choices.why: Right. Embedding was already the largest step locally, and a hosted API adds a trip over the internet that no database tuning touches.

choices.text: Switch to a smaller model, because 384 dimensions are too many to compare
choices.why: Comparing 384 numbers per vector is the cheap part; the measurement should come before any change.

prompt: Which of these does a vector database add over a NumPy matrix saved as a `.npy` file? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of these no store can give.

choices.text: An id kept in the same record as its vector
choices.why: Yes. The record carries its id, so no separate list can drift out of order.

choices.text: Changing or deleting one record without rebuilding the rest
choices.why: Yes. Upsert and delete work on one id, with tombstones and compaction behind them.

choices.text: Filters on metadata in the same query
choices.why: Yes. The metadata sits beside the vector, so the filter is part of the search.

choices.text: Scores more accurate than exact search
choices.why: Exact search is the reference; an approximate index can only match it or fall short.

choices.text: Vectors that stay valid when the model changes
choices.why: A new model means new vectors in any database; lesson 10's migration is the same everywhere.

prompt: A team tries an approximate index on 10,000 of its vectors. How should it judge whether the index's answers are good enough?
hint: What is the yardstick this lesson named?

choices.text: By its speed alone, since an index exists to be fast
choices.why: A fast index that returns the wrong neighbours is worse than a slow correct one; speed is half the measurement.

choices.text: By the share of its top results that match exact search's
choices.why: Right. On the same queries, exact search returns the true nearest vectors, so it is the reference; lesson 15 names this measure.

choices.text: By the scores it returns: higher scores mean better answers
choices.why: Scores depend on the vectors, not on the index; an index that misses the best match returns lower scores without saying so.

choices.text: By the size of the index file
choices.why: Size is a cost, not a measure of whether the answers are right.

hint: One description belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: Records of one model, one dimension, one comparison
Replace the record if the id exists, add it if not
A deleted record still in place, marked dead
